stances.claim: Jesus is a servant-leader by example -- anyone aspiring to greatness must serve, and Jesus modeled this by washing His apostles' feet despite being addressed as Teacher and Lord -- a model the Gentiles' lording-it-over leadership pattern violates.

Filipino politicians, despite being elected and calling themselves 'public servants,' arrogate to themselves power and authority over the life and death of the people -- dispensing patronage via pork barrel funds ('or whatever it is now called'), gatekeeping business openings and employment, and inserting themselves as wedding and baptism sponsors -- the opposite of Jesus's servant-leader model.

Jesus is a leader of intense prayer (Mt 14:23 mountain prayer, Gethsemane bloody-sweat prayer, crucifixion prayers 'Father, forgive them' and 'Father, into Your Hands I commend my spirit') and the Lord's Prayer is the best prayer of all -- taught by Jesus Himself.

Jesus is the ultimate judge -- Matthew 25:31-40 tests judgment on the canonical works (food, drink, clothing, comfort to the imprisoned) -- and the story of the adulteress (John 8) shows that justice is wisdom but love is supreme; 'Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone.'
stances.rhetorical_move: justice-with-love supremacy framing using two scripture passages

stances.claim: The supremacy of love over all other virtues -- speech, faith-to-move-mountains, almsgiving, even martyrdom -- is canonically expressed in 1 Corinthians 13: 'There are in the end three things that last: faith, hope, and love, and the greatest of these is love.'

notable_anecdotes: The lord-it-over critique of Filipino politicians -- 'though they call themselves public servants, yet they arrogate unto themselves power and authority over the life and death of our people' -- paired with the wedding/baptism/business-blessing inventory that makes the scriptural critique unmistakably PH-specific.
The pork-barrel parenthesis -- 'huge pork barrel funds, or whatever it is now called' -- CJ's quiet acknowledgment that the funds keep getting renamed without changing function.
Jesus's bloody-sweat Gethsemane prayer -- paired with the crucifixion prayers -- used as the prayer-life intensity catalog.

The adultery-stoning dilemma -- Jesus 'in the face of the dilemma' replying 'Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone at her' -- used as the canonical example of justice-with-love supremacy via the exposure of accusers' own sins.

1 Corinthians 13 quoted at length -- 'If I speak with human and angelic tongues but not have love, I am a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal... faith great enough to move mountains, but have no love, I gain nothing... give everything to feed the poor... but have no love, I am nothing... faith, hope, and love, and the greatest of these is love' -- CJ's most extensive Pauline citation, anchoring the love-supreme thesis.
Romans 14:17 -- 'the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating or drinking, but of justice, peace, and the joy that is given by the Holy Spirit' -- the canonical pairing of justice with joy and peace.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing Part 2 of his Christmas-season sharing before a Catholic charismatic community, Panganiban completes the five-way reflection on Jesus Christ as leader. Third -- Jesus is a servant-leader who leads by example: 'You know how among the Gentiles who seem to exercise authority lord it over them; their great ones make their importance felt. It cannot be like that with you... The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve' (Mark 10:42-45). CJ turns the scriptural standard against Filipino politicians who, though elected and calling themselves public servants, 'arrogate unto themselves power and authority over the life and death of our people' -- allocating huge 'pork barrel funds, or whatever it is now called' for patronage, gatekeeping business openings and employment, and inserting themselves into weddings and baptisms as sponsors. Quite the opposite, Jesus washed the apostles' feet (John 13:13-15), modeling that 'as I have done for you, so you must do.' Fourth -- Jesus is a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith: He went up the mountain alone to pray (Matthew 14:23), at Gethsemane prayed so intensely 'his sweat became like drops of blood,' and on the cross prayed aloud 'Father, forgive them for they know not what they do' and 'Father, into Your Hands I commend my spirit'; He Himself taught the Lord's Prayer as the best of all. Fifth and most importantly -- Jesus is a leader of justice AND love. The kingdom of God is not eating or drinking but 'justice, peace, and the joy that is given by the Holy Spirit' (Romans 14:17). He is the ultimate judge (Matthew 25:31-40) testing on food, drink, clothing, and comfort to the imprisoned. But he is also supremely compassionate -- confronted with the adulteress (John 8:1-11) facing Mosaic stoning, He replied 'Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone at her,' and the accusers dispersed because Jesus knew their sins. 'To be just is to be wise. But justice is not the most valued virtue in the kingdom of God. It is love.' As St. Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 13: 'If I speak with human and angelic tongues but not have love, I am a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal... if I have faith great enough to move mountains, but have no love, I gain nothing... If I give everything I have to feed the poor and hand over my body to be burned but have no love, I am nothing... There are in the end three things that last: faith, hope, and love, and the greatest of these is love.'
